0.0.n: Connects this remark to what the speaker was saying before.

0.2.n: A conversational filler that softens the transition to a new topic.

0.3.n: Often means a meal rather than just cooked rice; here the meal is dinner.

0.4.n: A casual contraction of と言ったら, not a form of つる here.

0.5.n: Invites the listener along as the speaker introduces the topic.

1.0.n: A casual, relatively gentle self-reference used mainly by men.

1.2.n: Refers to a short time before the present conversation.

1.3.n: Links さっき to 豚キムチ, identifying the dish as the one from earlier.

1.4.n: Adds a conversational pause inside the phrase さっきの豚キムチ.

1.6.n: Literally means pig, but names the meat in this dish.

1.7.n: Together with 豚, names a pork-and-kimchi dish.

1.8.n: Marks the pork kimchi as what remains.

1.9.n: Shows that the leftovers continue to be available now.

1.10.n: Short for 残っている, describing the continuing state of food remaining.

1.11.n: Short for の; adds an explanatory tone before です.

1.12.n: Makes the explanation polite rather than changing its basic content.

1.13.n: Presents the information as something the listener may not already know.

2.0.n: Introduces a reservation about eating the leftovers again.

2.1.n: Softens the transition into the speaker’s concern.

2.3.n: Points to the leftover pork kimchi being discussed.

2.4.n: Before １回, indicates an additional occasion rather than already.

2.5.n: The number １ plus 回 counts one occurrence; もう１回 means once more.

2.7.n: Names the meat component of 豚キムチ.

2.8.n: Combines with 豚 to name the dish the speaker would eat again.

2.9.n: Describes eating the leftovers without changing or adapting the dish.

2.10.n: The plain form describes the proposed action before っていうのは.

2.11.n: Casual form of という, introducing the action as something to discuss.

2.12.n: Turns the preceding action into a noun-like phrase that can be the topic.

2.13.n: Marks eating the dish again as the topic, with the judgment coming later.

3.0.n: Softens an implied negative reaction instead of stating it directly.

3.1.n: Adds a gentle conversational pause while the speaker hesitates.

3.3.n: The speaker refers to himself with the same casual pronoun used earlier.

3.4.n: Includes the speaker among people who would find this excessive.

3.5.n: With に, conveys that repeating the meal reaches a limit even the speaker acknowledges.

3.6.n: Completes さすがに, allowing it to comment on the speaker’s reaction.

4.0.n: 回 counts occurrences, here the number of meals eaten.

4.1.n: After ３回, shows that the three occasions are consecutive.

4.2.n: Directly modifies ご飯 without needing の.

4.3.n: Refers to the whole meal, not specifically rice.

4.4.n: Marks the same meal as what gets eaten.

4.5.n: The plain form describes the repeated action being evaluated.

4.6.n: Casual という introduces eating the same meal repeatedly as the matter under discussion.

4.7.n: Makes the preceding description of eating function like a noun.

4.8.n: Sets up the repeated eating as the topic for the next line’s judgment.

5.0.n: Softens the complaint and helps the speaker avoid sounding too negative.

5.1.n: Identifies the aspect of the meal that becomes an issue.

5.2.n: Marks 味 as what the vague description あれです applies to.

5.4.n: A vague stand-in for an awkward description, implying the flavor would become tiresome.

5.5.n: Adds politeness to the deliberately vague description あれ.

5.6.n: Gives the reason for changing the leftovers into a different dish.

6.0.n: Sets the time frame for the speaker’s new cooking plan.

6.2.n: Modifies ふう and points to the approach being shown or described.

6.3.n: Combines with こういう and に to describe how the speaker will proceed.

6.4.n: Makes こういうふう describe the manner of the planned preparation.

6.5.n: Usually names stir-fried noodles; here it refers to noodles used to adapt the leftovers.

6.6.n: Marks the noodles as the means or ingredient for making the new dish.

6.7.n: Keeps the listener engaged during a pause before naming the planned dish.

7.0.n: Names the meat component of the proposed noodle dish.

7.1.n: Names the kimchi component in the compound dish name.

7.2.n: Completes 豚キムチ焼きそば, the name of the dish the speaker plans to make.

7.4.n: Makes the proposed dish sound approximate rather than firmly decided.

7.5.n: Refers back to the pork kimchi noodle dish just mentioned.

7.6.n: Stands in for a dish after そういう.

7.7.n: Marks that kind of dish as what the speaker will try making.

7.8.n: 作って is the て-form of 作る; みよう adds the intention to try doing it.

7.9.n: Introduces the proposed plan as the content of the speaker’s thought.

7.10.n: Part of というふうに, which loosely frames how the speaker is thinking.

7.11.n: Links the phrasing ending in ふう to 思います as a way of thinking.

7.12.n: Polite form of 思う; with 作ってみよう, it expresses the speaker’s intention.

0.lit: And, well, speaking of dinner, you know…
0.tip: つったら is a very casual contraction of と言ったら, used here to introduce a topic.

1.lit: I—the pork kimchi from earlier, you know, still remains, you see.
1.tip: 残ってる describes a remaining state and is shortened from 残っている.

2.lit: However, you know, as for eating this pork kimchi once more as is…
2.tip: っていうのは turns the preceding action into a topic whose evaluation comes later.

3.lit: A bit, you know, even I, at that point…
3.tip: さすがに signals that something has reached a limit the speaker cannot comfortably accept.

4.lit: As for eating the same meal three times in a row…
4.tip: ３回連続 means three consecutive times, not merely three times in total.

5.lit: Because the taste is a bit, well, that.
5.tip: あれ tactfully replaces a negative description, leaving the listener to infer that the flavor would become tiresome.

6.lit: This time, in this way, using yakisoba noodles, you know…
6.tip: で marks what the speaker will use to transform the leftovers.

7.lit: Pork kimchi yakisoba—something like that, I think I’ll try making.
7.tip: A form ending in よう followed by と思います expresses an intention: I think I’ll do it.
